comparator.name: Astronomy
comparator.sourceNotes: The 2026–2027 regulations define a 150 EC Astronomy major and a 30 EC free minor. Astronomy and Astronomy Instrumentation and Informatics are optional deepening minors within that space. The regulations set the research-project entry requirements.
components: Introduction to Programming and Computational Methods
Take Introduction to Programming and Computational Methods first. The course includes an observing project with Groningen’s Gratama Telescope.
Builds on Calculus 1 and Linear Algebra.
Choose a 30 EC minor. Groningen offers optional deepening minors in Astronomy and in Astronomy Instrumentation and Informatics.
Normally requires 150 EC. Third-year Astronomy students who earn 135 EC within their first three years of registration may also start.

core: Calculus, linear algebra, probability and numerical modelling for scientific problems
Programming, algorithms and analysis of scientific data and images
Wave behaviour, remote sensing, signal processing and computational control as related methods for observation and instrumentation
Empirical research design, statistical inference and analysis of measured data
adjacent: Geology, geophysical measurements and interpretation of Earth observation data

trace: Designs empirical studies, checks measurement quality and uses statistical inference in a team project.
Models decisions under uncertainty and partial observability, extending the programme from observed data to decisions by autonomous agents.
Uses logic, sets, relations, induction and recursion to formulate and analyse mathematical and computational problems.
Implements and evaluates search and numerical optimisation, including local optimisation and constrained problems.
Investigates data communication and computing infrastructure through network measurements and operating-system performance experiments.
Models relational data, constructs SQL queries and normalises databases to organise and retrieve datasets.
Designs and tests algorithms, compares running times and reports experimental performance.
Imports, cleans, joins and visualises data in R, including spatial data.
Fits and validates statistical learning models and evaluates prediction on held-out data.
Uses spatial and spectral representations, filtering and feature detection to build and test image-processing pipelines.
Trains and evaluates neural networks, including applications to images and time series.
Models robot motion, programmes a robot arm and introduces sensing and control through kinematics and motion planning.
Writes, tests and debugs Python programmes for structured computational problems.
Uses single-variable calculus, complex numbers and differential equations in a dynamic modelling project.
Uses matrices, vector spaces, linear transformations and eigenvalues, with applications to signals and dynamical systems.
Implements numerical integration, interpolation, root finding and differential-equation solvers and compares error and stability.
Extends calculus to multiple variables and differential equations, including complex-valued functions.
Models continuous and discrete signals and systems using differential equations, Fourier analysis, sampling and filtering.
Uses probability, estimation, hypothesis tests, Bayesian reasoning and simulations to evaluate uncertainty.
Uses geological observation, field measurements and seismology to interpret Earth processes that provide context for remote sensing.
Processes georeferenced observations and spectral data to study Earth systems through remote sensing and GIS.
Uses uncertainty, dynamic models and practical measurements to study Earth systems and environmental processes.
Investigates electromagnetic and mechanical waves, interference, Fourier analysis and optical spectroscopy in an environmental and materials context.

alternatives.label: Scientific computing, mathematical modelling & observation data
alternatives.concept: Learn to model systems, analyse data and process images and signals. Apply these skills to Earth observation and explore how robots sense and move.
alternatives.labelReason: Calculus, numerical modelling, statistics, programming, imaging and signal processing anchor the programme. Geology, remote sensing and robotics provide applied settings.
progression: Programming and scientific data foundations come first. Mathematical Methods precedes advanced mathematics and robotics. Sustainability Essentials I precedes waves and materials work in Sustainability Essentials II and precedes Earth Observation. Image processing and machine learning precede deep learning.

candidates.label: Astrophysics, cosmology, galaxies, stars and planetary systems
Radio astronomy and experimental astronomical observation

selection.assessment: One related programme combines numerical modelling, scientific data and observation methods with Earth sensing and robotic applications. A separate astrophysics direction lacks sustained physics and astronomy. A separate radio astronomy direction lacks telescopes, radio measurement and astronomical observing practice. General computing or Earth science can deepen the related programme but would leave those disciplinary gaps in a second option.

blocks: Both use single-variable differentiation and integration, Taylor expansions and elementary differential equations. Groningen emphasises physical applications.
Both develop matrices, systems of equations, vector spaces, linear maps and eigenvalues.
Both implement interpolation, numerical integration, root finding and numerical solutions to differential equations. Groningen uses Python for methods common in astronomical research.
Both extend calculus to several variables. Groningen specifically develops vector fields and integral theorems used in physics.
Both use differential equations and Fourier analysis to study systems. Groningen also introduces partial differential equations in physics. UCR concentrates on signals, filters and feedback.
Both develop probability, Bayesian inference and hypothesis testing. Groningen applies statistics and error analysis to astronomical data.
Both introduce programming for computational problems. Groningen uses the course as preparation for Observational Astronomy.

Both work with acquired observations, spectral information and data processing. UCR focuses on Earth remote sensing and mapping. Groningen uses telescopes, photometry and spectroscopy in an astronomical observing project.
Both investigate wave behaviour and interference through practical work. Groningen gives dedicated treatment to electromagnetic waves, optics and the mathematical description of these phenomena.
Astronomy, physics, laboratory work, minor and research
Groningen sets aside 30 EC for a minor. The specific courses depend on the student’s choice.
Groningen requires a supervised Astronomy research project. UCR’s optional independent research is outside the scheduled 180 EC.

notes.text: The UCR option shares some mathematics, computing, wave physics and methods for analysing observations. Groningen also requires mechanics, electromagnetism, quantum and thermal physics, telescope observing, specialist astronomy courses and a supervised Astronomy research project.

audience.programmeDescription: Astronomy at the University of Groningen uses physics, mathematics and observation to study planets, stars, galaxies and the matter between them. Students plan observations, analyse astronomical data and complete an individual research project.
audience.comparisonExplanation: UCR offers related training in modelling, signals and image analysis. Its observation work focuses on Earth, while Groningen trains students to use telescopes and investigate astronomical systems.
